abstract: Jinjiimaa Otgonsuren examines AI's systemic impact on labor relations and employment structures, arguing that industries with high volumes of structured, repetitive tasks face the sharpest near-term employment contractions. The paper maps how AI is reshaping the employer-employee relationship across multiple dimensions: hiring practices (algorithmic screening), performance management (continuous AI monitoring), task allocation (human-AI workflow redesign), and collective bargaining dynamics (reduced worker leverage as automation alternatives become viable). The analysis emphasizes that AI's impact on labor relations extends beyond simple job displacement to fundamentally alter the power dynamics between workers and employers. Industries identified as most immediately affected include manufacturing operations, financial services back-office, customer service, and administrative support functions where tasks can be clearly defined and measured.
keyFindings: Industries with high volumes of structured, repetitive tasks face the sharpest near-term employment contractions from AI.
AI reshapes labor relations across multiple dimensions: hiring, performance management, task allocation, and collective bargaining.
Automation alternatives reduce worker leverage in collective bargaining even before actual displacement occurs.
Most immediately affected industries include manufacturing operations, financial services back-office, customer service, and administrative support.
AI's labor impact extends beyond displacement to fundamentally alter employer-employee power dynamics.
methodology: Academic paper using structured literature review and theoretical framework analysis to map AI's multi-dimensional impact on labor relations and employment structures. Published in a peer-reviewed academic context via Semantic Scholar.
qualifiers: The paper is primarily theoretical and framework-based rather than empirically grounded in original data. The claim about 'sharpest near-term contractions' in structured/repetitive task industries aligns with conventional expectations but may underweight AI's emerging capability in unstructured cognitive work. Full paper content was not available through Semantic Scholar's abstract page; findings are based on the abstract and available metadata. Geographic and institutional scope of the analysis is unclear from available information.
